title: Cost control, EMR Serverless, architecture trade-offs
exp: Cost and architecture decisions distinguish a developer who built a Spark job from one who can own a production data platform. These are Lead I questions.
pts: Spot fleet with multiple instance types for better availability.
EMR Serverless: no cluster; pay per vCPU-second; ~30-90s cold start. Best for infrequent jobs.
AWS Glue: serverless ETL, simpler for small jobs, less control than EMR.
When Spark is overkill: a 50MB CSV daily does not need EMR -- pandas on Lambda is simpler and cheaper.

viz.note: Decision matrix: 50MB daily -> pandas Lambda. 10GB daily -> small EMR. 1TB daily -> EMR transient. 10TB hourly -> EMR persistent with auto-scaling task nodes.

qa.q: When would you choose EMR Serverless over EMR on EC2?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** EMR Serverless for infrequent jobs, variable workloads, teams with no cluster expertise, pay-per-use billing. EMR on EC2 for frequent jobs where a persistent cluster amortizes startup, complex tuning, Spot strategies. The JD's 50-source daily pipeline with hours of processing favors EMR on EC2.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Operating When would you choose EMR Serverless over EMR on EC2? at scale requires understanding the runtime lifecycle, memory allocations, and underlying execution constraints. The underlying framework or storage engine optimizes execution when contracts are explicitly preserved.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Un-handled edge cases in When would you choose EMR Serverless over EMR on EC2? under high concurrent traffic can lead to performance degradation, unhandled exceptions, or unexpected memory growth. Always enforce defensive validation and error handling.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Choosing this implementation approach balances developer velocity and system performance. Senior engineers evaluate latency, operational overhead, and maintenance costs before committing.

**Elevator Pitch:** When data fits in memory on one machine. Spark adds startup overhead (2-10 min), operational complexity, higher cost. A 50MB CSV daily is better served by pandas on Lambda. Use Spark when data genuinely does not fit on one machine.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Boxing allocates a System.Object header (16 bytes on x64) on the managed heap and copies the value type bytes into it. Span<T> is a ref struct allocated strictly on the execution stack, providing contiguous memory access without heap allocation or array copying.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Boxing inside a high-throughput loop generates thousands of ephemeral Gen 0 objects, triggering frequent GC pauses and thread pool delays. Fix: use generic collection interfaces (IList<T>) and Span<T>/Memory<T> for byte slicing.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> provides zero-allocation performance, but ref struct rules forbid storing it on the heap, as class fields, or across async await points (where Memory<T> must be used).
